Q: Excel - paste special HTML option A:

This is maybe more code than you anticipated needing, but seems to function OK.

It uses Ron de Bruin's RangetoHTML function to create an HTML representation of the range to be copied, then adds a "wrapper" around that HTML before placing it on the clipboard. The "wrapper" around the HTML allows Excel to recognize that the clipboard has content in HTML format.

Background on the HTML "wrapper" at this link:
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/dataxchg/html-clipboard-format

See here for the RangetoHTML function:
https://jkp-ads.com/rdb/win/s1/outlook/bmail2.htm .

Sub TestCopyRangeAsHtml()
    
    Dim html As String, ws As Worksheet
    
    Set ws = ActiveSheet
    
    'convert the source range to HTML
    html = RangetoHTML(ws.Range("B2:E6")) 'See https://jkp-ads.com/rdb/win/s1/outlook/bmail2.htm

   'Note: this approach also supports pasting of hard-coded or dynamic 
   '    HTML fragments from other sources, such as the table below
   ' html = "<BODY><TABLE BORDER><TR><TH ROWSPAN=2>Head1</TH><TD>Item 1</TD>" & _
   '        "<TD>Item 2</TD><TD>Item 3</TD><TD>Item 4</TD></TR><TR><TD>Item 5</TD>" & _
   '        "<TD>Item 6</TD><TD>Item 7</TD><TD>Item 8</TD></TR><TR><TH>Head2</TH>" & _
   '        "<TD>Item 9</TD><TD>Item 10</TD><TD>Item 11</TD><TD>Item 12</TD></TR>" & _
   '        "</TABLE></BODY>"


    set_clipboard_text wrapHTML(html)     'put wrapped HTML in the clipboard
    
    ws.Range("G2").Select    'must select before pasting
    ActiveSheet.PasteSpecial 'paste as HTML
End Sub

'See: https://stackoverflow.com/a/63735992/478884
'The "wrapper" lets Excel know the clipboard format is HTML
Private Function wrapHTML(ByVal html As String) As String
    Dim sData As String
    Const sContextStart = "<HTML><BODY><!--StartFragment -->"
    Const sContextEnd = "<!--EndFragment --></BODY></HTML>"
    Const sHtmlHeader = _
            "Version:1.0" & vbCrLf & _
            "StartHTML:<{]aaaaaaa" & vbCrLf & _
            "EndHTML:<{]bbbbbbb" & vbCrLf & _
            "StartFragment:<{]ccccccc" & vbCrLf & _
            "EndFragment:<{]dddddddd" + vbCrLf
    sData = sHtmlHeader & sContextStart & html & sContextEnd
    sData = Replace(sData, "<{]aaaaaaa", Format(Len(sHtmlHeader), "0000000000"))
    sData = Replace(sData, "<{]bbbbbbb", Format(Len(sData), "0000000000"))
    sData = Replace(sData, "<{]ccccccc", Format(Len(sHtmlHeader & sContextStart), "0000000000"))
    sData = Replace(sData, "<{]ddddddd", Format(Len(sHtmlHeader & sContextStart & html), "0000000000"))
    wrapHTML = sData
End Function

'https://stackoverflow.com/a/78329329/478884
Function set_clipboard_text(str_text)
    On Error GoTo err_handler
    Dim MSForms_DataObject As Object
    Set MSForms_DataObject = CreateObject("new:{1C3B4210-F441-11CE-B9EA-00AA006B1A69}")
    MSForms_DataObject.SetText str_text
    MSForms_DataObject.PutInClipboard
    Set MSForms_DataObject = Nothing
    set_clipboard_text = True
    Exit Function
err_handler:
    Debug.Print "error in set_clipboard_text function. Err: " & _
    Err.description
set_clipboard_text = False
End Function

Q: Find and kill a process in one line using Bash and regular expressions A:

You can do it with AWK and backticks:

ps auxf | grep 'python csp_build.py' | `awk '{ print "kill " $2 }'`

$2 in AWK prints column 2, and the backticks runs the statement that's printed.

But a much cleaner solution would be for the python process to store its process ID in /var/run and then you can simply read that file and kill it.

Q: Why is it the number 9 in the 'kill -9' command on Unix? A:

I think a better answer here is simply this:

kill -l

Output:

 1) SIGHUP       2) SIGINT       3) SIGQUIT      4) SIGILL       5) SIGTRAP
 6) SIGABRT      7) SIGBUS       8) SIGFPE       9) SIGKILL     10) SIGUSR1
11) SIGSEGV     12) SIGUSR2     13) SIGPIPE     14) SIGALRM     15) SIGTERM
16) SIGSTKFLT   17) SIGCHLD     18) SIGCONT     19) SIGSTOP     20) SIGTSTP
21) SIGTTIN     22) SIGTTOU     23) SIGURG      24) SIGXCPU     25) SIGXFSZ
26) SIGVTALRM   27) SIGPROF     28) SIGWINCH    29) SIGIO       30) SIGPWR
31) SIGSYS      34) SIGRTMIN    35) SIGRTMIN+1  36) SIGRTMIN+2  37) SIGRTMIN+3
38) SIGRTMIN+4  39) SIGRTMIN+5  40) SIGRTMIN+6  41) SIGRTMIN+7  42) SIGRTMIN+8
43) SIGRTMIN+9  44) SIGRTMIN+10 45) SIGRTMIN+11 46) SIGRTMIN+12 47) SIGRTMIN+13
48) SIGRTMIN+14 49) SIGRTMIN+15 50) SIGRTMAX-14 51) SIGRTMAX-13 52) SIGRTMAX-12
53) SIGRTMAX-11 54) SIGRTMAX-10 55) SIGRTMAX-9  56) SIGRTMAX-8  57) SIGRTMAX-7
58) SIGRTMAX-6  59) SIGRTMAX-5  60) SIGRTMAX-4  61) SIGRTMAX-3  62) SIGRTMAX-2
63) SIGRTMAX-1  64) SIGRTMAX

As for the "significance" of 9... I would say there is probably none. According to The Linux Programming Interface(p 388):

Each signal is defined as a unique (small) integer, starting sequentially from 1. These integers are defined in <signal.h> with symbolic names of the form SIGxxxx . Since the actual numbers used for each signal vary across implementations, it is these symbolic names that are always used in programs.
